subfield: Condensed matter and materials physics / photovoltaics
motivation: Miyasaka first used methylammonium lead halide perovskites as photovoltaic absorbers (2009). Park (2012) and Snaith (2012) then turned them into long-lived solid-state devices. Snaith's meso-superstructured and planar thin-film cells showed that these solution-processed semiconductors carry both electrons and holes over long distances, with sharp absorption edges and unusual tolerance to defects. This physics was unexpected in a material made at low temperature, and it overturned established views on how crystalline perfection limits photovoltaic performance. In little more than a decade, cell efficiencies rose from 3.8% to over 26%, and perovskite–silicon tandems now exceed the Shockley–Queisser limit for single-junction silicon. Perovskites have opened a new field in semiconductor physics and have reached commercial tandem modules, which promise cheap, abundant solar electricity. This discovery is of great benefit to humankind, as Nobel intended.
